extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of journalism, social scientists, policymakers, and concerned citizens
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for assessing the quality and responsibilities of newspapers, journalists, and experts in democratic society — including distinctions between news and truth, sourcing standards, the role of stereotypes and attention, and the proper work and posture of experts/social scientists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper selection and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Every newspaper when it reaches the reader is the result of a whole series of selections as to what items shall be printed, in what position they shall be printed, how much space each shall occupy, what emphasis each shall have. There are no objective standards here. There are conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors' choices depend on judgment about what will absorb the readers' limited attention; presentation (headlines, placement, emphasis) shapes perception. Example contrast: different headlines on same morning produce very different reader responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Securing attention vs. ethical/perspective reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem of securing attention is by no means equivalent to displaying the news in the perspective laid down by religious teaching or by some form of ethical culture. It is a problem of provoking feeling in the reader, of inducing him to feel a sense of personal identification with the stories he is reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News often aims to provoke feeling and identification to engage readers; this incentive can conflict with ethical or comprehensive portrayal of events and should be recognized when evaluating reporting choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stereotypes as cues for reader identification
rubrics_metrics.description: In order that [the reader] shall enter he must find a familiar foothold in the story, and this is supplied to him by the use of stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stereotypes act as cues (e.g., calling a plumbers' association a 'combine' vs a 'group of leading business men' signals hostility or favor). Recognize that stereotypes facilitate quick reader identification but also channel opinion and can distort complex realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorials as interpretive cues when news is confusing
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes in a situation that on the news pages is too confusing to permit of identification, [editorials] give the reader a clue by means of which he engages himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorials should help readers integrate confusing news by suggesting interpretations or perspectives; this function is to guide reader engagement, but editors must manage transitions and changes of position carefully to avoid betraying readership expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between news and truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis ... is that news and truth are not the same thing, and must be clearly distinguished. The function of news is to signalize an event, the function of truth is to bring to light the hidden facts, to set them into relation with each other, and make a picture of reality on which men can act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate reporting by whether it merely signals events or attempts the deeper work of uncovering underlying facts and relations; don't conflate timely event-reporting with comprehensive truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability of source and accurate qualification of reports
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no defense ... for stating six times that Lenin is dead, when the only information the paper possesses is a report that he is dead from a source repeatedly shown to be unreliable. The news ... is not 'Lenin Dead' but 'Helsingfors Says Lenin is Dead.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers must judge the reliability of sources and avoid overstating certainty; properly qualify reports by source and reliability rather than asserting unverified facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize topics lacking exact tests
rubrics_metrics.description: But when it comes to dealing, for example, with stories of what the Russian people want, no such test exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For some subjects (e.g., collective wants, attitudes) exact verification tests are absent; journalists should acknowledge uncertainty and avoid presenting speculative conclusions as settled fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of journalistic discipline beyond recorded facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Once he departs from the region where it is definitely recorded ... all fixed standards disappear. The story of why John Smith failed ... all of this can be told in a hundred different ways. There is no discipline in applied psychology ... which has authority to direct the journalist's mind when he passes from the news to the vague realm of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appraise features and interpretive pieces with the understanding that outside clearly recorded events there are no coercive objective canons; such pieces are versions and interpretations, not demonstrable truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists should temper assurance and admit subjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: He knows that he is seeing the world through subjective lenses. He cannot deny that he too is ... a dome of many-colored glass which stains the white radiance of eternity. And by this knowledge his assurance is tempered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice includes awareness of personal and institutional biases and restraint in claiming certainty where objective tests are lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press quality as an index of social organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Therefore, on the whole, the quality of the news about modern society is an index of its social organization. The better the institutions, the more all interests concerned are formally represented, the more issues are disentangled, the more objective criteria are introduced, the more perfectly an affair can be presented as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the press, consider the underlying institutional record-keeping and representation: stronger institutions enable more objective, disentangled reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press cannot substitute for institutions or continuous analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The press is no substitute for institutions. It is like the beam of a searchlight that moves restlessly about, bringing one episode and then another out of darkness into vision. Men cannot do the work of the world by this light alone. They cannot govern society by episodes, incidents, and eruptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess expectations placed on media: criticism should account for the press's episodic nature and the need for steady institutional analysis and record to support democratic decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for systems of analysis and record to improve public knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The trouble lies deeper than the press, and so does the remedy. It lies in social organization based on a system of analysis and record ... in the coordination of decision by comparable record and analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvements in public information must come from institutional reforms: audits, comparable records, decentralized decision-making and better data flows — not solely from journalistic exertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experts should break stereotypes and present impersonal factual pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: They reverse the process by which interesting public opinions are built up. Instead of presenting a casual fact, a large screen of stereotypes, and a dramatic identification, they break down the drama, break through the stereotypes, and offer men a picture of facts, which is unfamiliar and to them impersonal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value expert work that resists sensational stereotypes and provides impersonal, systematic presentations of facts even if such presentations are dull or painful to lay audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social scientists must develop method and usable instruments of analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The social scientist will acquire his dignity and his strength when he has worked out his method. He will do that by turning into opportunity the need among directing men of the Great Society for instruments of analysis by which an invisible [world] is made intelligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess social science by the rigor and practical applicability of its methods; emphasis on comparable data, records, and methods that can inform decision-makers in real contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experts should supply facts before decisions (not only ex post facto)
rubrics_metrics.description: The real sequence should be one where the disinterested expert first finds and formulates the facts for the man of action, and later makes what wisdom he can out of comparison between the decision ... and the facts, which he organized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good expert practice: provide organized factual bases to decision-makers prior to action; avoid serving merely as later rationalizers for decisions already taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert reports must translate, simplify, generalize, and be applicable in context
rubrics_metrics.description: The expert must translate, simplify, generalize, but the inference from the result must apply in the East, not merely on the premises of the report. ... The last thing they expect to find is a neat argument justifying the American position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating expert analyses, check for contextual applicability and avoidance of normative bias; reports should represent what different actors think and are likely to do, not advocate a predetermined policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experts must maintain disinterestedness to preserve credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of the expert depends upon separating himself from those who make the decisions, upon not caring, in his expert self, what decision is made. The man who ... takes a line, and meddles with the decision, is soon discounted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An expert who shows partisan commitment or excessive attachment to outcomes will be seen as biased and lose effectiveness; impartiality and representation of unseen factors are central to expert authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experts represent invisible interests and make them visible
rubrics_metrics.description: He represents people who are not voters, functions of voters that are not evident, events that are out of sight, mute people, unborn people, relations between things and people. He has a constituency of intangibles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate expert work by its success in rendering invisible or unrepresented elements visible (e.g., comparative statistics, administrative records) so they can be taken into account by decision-makers and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comparative statistics to create visibility and prompt corrective action
rubrics_metrics.description: The printing of comparative statistics of infant mortality is often followed by a reduction of the death rate of babies. Municipal officials and voters did not have, before publication, a place in their picture of the environment for those babies. The statistics made them visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and favor reporting and research that provides comparable, public statistics which reveal overlooked problems and thereby enable policy response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical engagement of experts with action fosters experimental social science
rubrics_metrics.description: These practical students are the true pioneers of a new social science. They are 'in mesh with the driving wheels' and from this practical engagement of science and action, both will benefit radically ... the number of comparable experiences begins to approach the dimensions of genuine experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value expert work embedded with practical decision-making because it creates opportunities for comparable cases, low-risk trial-and-error, and cumulative learning across institutions.
